title: Indoor Climbing Walls
one_liner: Indoor climbing gyms sell access to artificial climbing terrain, instruction and community-based fitness experiences.
overview: Operators run indoor climbing and bouldering facilities with artificial walls, padded bouldering areas, ropes, auto-belays, training zones and related fitness programming. The category benefits from climbing's fitness, social and youth-sport appeal, its Olympic visibility and the continued expansion of gyms into suburban and underserved markets. The business remains capital intensive because facilities require specialized buildouts, large leased spaces, route-setting labor, insurance and safety systems. In 2025, the industry was still growing in capacity, but operator sentiment weakened as expenses rose and many mature gyms reported flat or lower revenue and traffic.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 US climbing gym revenue: $1.123 billion; 2026 estimate: $1.224 billion
key_stats.growth: 2026-2033 US revenue CAGR forecast: 8.9%; 2025 North American net gym growth: 4.7%; 2025 US net gym growth: 4.2%
key_stats.facilities: 2025 North America: more than 900 climbing gyms; 2025 openings: 53 North America, including 40 in the US; 2025 closures: 12, all in the US
key_stats.participation: 2025 indoor climbing participation: 7.1 million US participants, up 13.1%; 2025 sport and boulder climbing participation: 3.2 million, up 20.1%
key_stats.largest_segment: 2025 US bouldering share: 44.56% of climbing gym revenue

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 baseline projection from 2021 IBISWorld report: about $512 million in 2021 dollars, derived from $492.9 million in 2021 revenue and a 3.8% 2021-2026 forecast CAGR
baseline_2022.growth: 2021 baseline forecast: 3.8% annualized revenue growth for 2021-2026; 2021 actual rebound was 14.2% after a 25.8% 2020 decline
baseline_2022.revenue_mix: 2021 baseline: memberships and day passes 69.8%, fitness programs 20.5%, retail merchandise 2.5%, other 7.2%

how_it_makes_money: Revenue comes primarily from monthly and annual memberships, day passes and punch cards. Operators add higher-margin revenue through beginner classes, youth teams, coaching, camps, birthday parties, corporate events, competitions, belay certification, gear rental, retail merchandise, food and beverage, yoga and strength classes.
cost_structure: Major costs are facility rent or mortgage payments, payroll for front desk staff, coaches and routesetters, wall construction and maintenance, holds and padding replacement, insurance, utilities, cleaning, software, marketing and debt service. Margins are pressured by large fixed occupancy costs and rising labor and insurance expenses, while dense membership utilization, youth programs and instruction improve operating leverage.
current_dynamics: The 2025 market is still expanding but is no longer in easy-growth mode. New facilities continued to open, especially bouldering and mixed gyms, but CBJ reported fewer openings and less new wall surface in 2025 than in 2024. Existing operators faced flatter revenue and traffic, higher expenses and pressure to professionalize pricing, staffing, programming and multi-site operations. Youth programs, coaching and flexible memberships are becoming more important to retention.
whats_growing: Bouldering remains the largest revenue segment, youth teams and recreational youth leagues are adding recurring demand, and indoor-only climbers are increasingly treating the gym as the main product rather than a gateway to outdoor climbing. Larger chains and well-capitalized operators are better positioned to add amenities, software, training spaces and multi-location memberships.
whats_shrinking: The pace of new-gym development slowed in 2025, and total climbing wall square footage added in North America fell from 460,997 square feet in 2024 to 356,314 square feet in 2025. Mature gyms are seeing more flat or down traffic, and expensive or poorly programmed specialty training equipment is less compelling when it displaces core climbing terrain.
recent_developments: 2025-02-09: CBJ reported North American climbing gyms rose to over 870 in 2024, with bouldering gyms accounting for 73% of new development.
2025-04-09: IFSC reported that LA28 will hold standalone Boulder, Lead and Speed Olympic medal events, raising sport climbing to six gold-medal events in 2028.
2026-01-09: CBJ named High Point Orlando the largest and tallest new climbing gym of 2025, with 35,000 square feet of climbing terrain and 52-foot walls.
2026-02-08: CBJ counted 53 North American climbing gym openings in 2025, including 40 in the US, and 12 permanent closures, all in the US.
2026-02-08: CBJ reported 2025 North American net gym growth of 4.7% and US net growth of 4.2%, down from 2024 growth rates.
2026-05-11: Grand View Research estimated 2025 US climbing gym revenue at $1.123 billion and 2026 revenue at $1.224 billion.
outlook: The industry should keep growing through 2026 as climbing participation, youth competition pipelines, urban/suburban facility expansion and LA28 visibility support demand. Growth is likely to be more disciplined than the immediate post-pandemic buildout because high rent, construction, financing, payroll and insurance costs raise breakeven utilization. The strongest operators will be those that convert casual trial visits into recurring memberships, run profitable youth and coaching programs, refresh routes consistently and manage fixed costs across multiple locations.
one_sentence: The US indoor climbing wall industry has moved from niche recreation into boutique fitness, but 2025 conditions were more uneven as higher operating costs, slower gym openings and flatter traffic tested operators after a strong post-pandemic expansion.

title: Indoor Sports Facilities Management
one_liner: Operators rent, program and maintain indoor courts, rinks, pools and turf fields for leagues, training, events and drop-in recreation.
overview: The industry consists of for-profit and nonprofit operators that maintain and operate indoor recreational sports facilities, excluding bowling alleys, college facilities and fitness centers whose core offer is exercise equipment. The 2022 baseline was still recovering from COVID-era closures, with revenue at $1.412 billion in 2022 and 4.0% growth in 2022 after a 26.8% revenue drop in 2020. Current demand conditions are stronger than the 2022 baseline suggested: SFIA reported 250 million Americans participating in at least one sport, fitness or leisure activity in 2025, team sports exceeded 90 million participants in 2025, indoor soccer reached 6.6 million participants in 2025, and recreation services PCE reached $819.215 billion in 2025. Operators are responding with multi-sport layouts, court conversions, rentals, tournaments, youth leagues, training programs and fee increases, but high fixed costs, staffing shortages and aging assets limit profitability.

key_stats.market_size: US revenue was $1.4 billion in 2024 according to an IBISWorld market-size citation, and an estimated $1.5 billion in 2025 based on 2024 industry revenue, 2024 market-size growth of 4.0%, 2025 recreation-services PCE growth and 2025 participation gains.
key_stats.growth: Market-size growth was 4.0% in 2024; 2025 growth is estimated at about 3.0% to 5.0% as recreation-services PCE rose from $777.049 billion in 2024 to $819.215 billion in 2025.
key_stats.participation: SFIA reported 250 million active Americans in 2025, up 1.2% year over year, with core participants at 158.8 million in 2025, up 1.3% year over year.
key_stats.team_sports: SFIA reported team sports surpassed 90 million total participants in 2025.
key_stats.indoor_soccer: SFIA reported 6.6 million indoor soccer participants in 2025, a record high.
key_stats.pickleball: SFIA reported 24.3 million pickleball participants in 2025, up from 4.2 million in 2020; pickleball grew 171.8% from 2022 to 2025.
key_stats.recreation_spending: BEA/FRED recreation-services PCE was $819.215 billion in 2025, up from $777.049 billion in 2024 and $677.298 billion in 2022.
key_stats.facility_usage: Recreation Management reported 57.3% of surveyed recreation, sports and fitness facilities had higher facility usage in 2025, while 57.5% expected usage to rise in 2026.
key_stats.operating_costs: Recreation Management respondents projected average operating costs rising from $4.21 million in 2025 to $4.33 million in 2026 and $4.56 million in 2027.

baseline_2022.growth: 4.0% revenue growth in 2022; revenue declined at a 1.3% annualized rate from 2017 to 2022 due to the 2020 COVID contraction.
baseline_2022.profit_margin: 11.5% profit margin in 2022, down from 13.2% in 2017.
baseline_2022.forecast: IBISWorld's 2022 baseline forecast called for 2.3% annualized revenue growth from 2022 to 2027, reaching $1.6 billion in 2027.

how_it_makes_money: Revenue comes from membership and admission fees, hourly court or field rentals, youth and adult league fees, tournaments, camps, coaching and training, birthday parties and private events, equipment rentals, pro-shop sales, concessions, vending, sponsorships and school or club partnerships. In the 2022 baseline, indoor ice rinks generated 23.7% of revenue, indoor soccer complexes 22.8%, indoor swimming complexes 19.4%, indoor basketball complexes 18.3%, indoor tennis courts 9.1% and other indoor sports facilities 6.7%. In 2026, Recreation Management reported rentals and private events as a funding source for 67.3% of surveyed facilities and membership or admission fees for 64.6%.
cost_structure: The cost base is fixed-asset heavy: rent or debt service, utilities, insurance, maintenance, cleaning, scheduling systems and frontline labor must be paid before utilization is known. The 2022 baseline showed $503 million in wages and an 11.5% profit margin. Ice rinks and pools carry especially high 2022-era climate-control, water-treatment and maintenance costs. In 2026, BLS reported amusement and recreation industry average hourly earnings of $25.98 in May 2026 and production/nonsupervisory earnings of $21.79 in May 2026. Recreation Management reported 54.4% of 2026 respondents cited equipment and facility maintenance as a top challenge, 53.2% cited staffing, 52.1% had increased fees to offset costs, and 33.9% had improved energy efficiency.
major_players: YMCA, JCC and nonprofit recreation-center operators
Regional indoor soccer, basketball, volleyball, pickleball and turf-complex operators
School, club and tournament partners that anchor facility schedules
current_dynamics: Demand is broadening in 2025-2026 because indoor facilities solve weather, scheduling and access constraints for youth sports, adult leagues, soccer, pickleball, basketball, volleyball, lacrosse, baseball training, swimming and ice sports. The strongest operators are using dense programming calendars, rentals, camps and tournaments to lift utilization outside evening peak hours. Inflation has pushed many facilities to raise fees, while staffing and maintenance remain the practical bottlenecks. Competition remains local and includes gyms, boutique fitness, outdoor public recreation space, school facilities, parks departments and entertainment venues.
whats_growing: Youth team sports, flag football, basketball, soccer, pickleball, padel, court rentals, private events, camps, club-team training, tournament hosting, facility-management software, automated booking, energy-efficiency upgrades and multi-sport complexes are growing. NSGA reported 2024 youth flag football participation was 21% above its three-year average and youth basketball was 12% above its three-year average. SFIA reported indoor soccer reached 6.6 million participants in 2025, pickleball reached 24.3 million participants in 2025, and padel reached about 1.07 million participants in 2025.
whats_shrinking: Single-sport facilities with weak off-peak utilization, underinvested rinks and pools, low-margin open-gym sessions, purely fitness-adjacent offers, and projects dependent on cheap financing are under pressure. Recreation Management reported only 32.3% of 2026 respondents planned to add facility features, the lowest level since 2010, while 29.1% had put construction plans on hold in 2026. Fitness-only substitutes remain a threat, and high-utility ice and aquatics facilities face more margin risk than flexible court and turf formats.
recent_developments: 2025-04-15: NSGA reported 2024 youth team sports gains, with flag football up 21% and basketball up 12% versus their three-year averages.
2026-03-12: SFIA reported 250 million Americans participated in a sport, fitness or leisure activity in 2025, the highest level in its tracking history.
2026-03-12: SFIA reported team sports surpassed 90 million participants in 2025, the strongest year-over-year growth category.
2026-06-04: SFIA reported 24.3 million US pickleball participants in 2025 and 1.07 million US padel participants in 2025.
2026-06-05: SFIA soccer data showed indoor soccer reached 6.6 million participants in 2025 and combined indoor/outdoor soccer participation reached about 25.5 million Americans by June 2026.
2026-06-08: Recreation Management reported 57.5% of surveyed facilities expected usage to increase in 2026, while 54.4% named maintenance and 53.2% named staffing as top challenges.
outlook: The 2026-2028 outlook is modestly positive, with demand supported by high participation, youth sports spending, soccer momentum around the 2026 World Cup, pickleball and padel adoption, and continued household spending on recreation services. Revenue growth should remain faster than the flat 2017-2022 baseline but constrained by fee sensitivity, wages, utilities, insurance and maintenance. Operators with flexible surfaces, strong scheduling discipline, school and club partnerships, tournament capacity and ancillary food, retail or training revenue should outperform single-purpose facilities. A reasonable 2027 revenue range is $1.55 billion to $1.65 billion, consistent with the 2022 IBISWorld forecast of $1.6 billion in 2027 and newer 2025-2026 participation indicators.
themes: Soccer momentum before and during the 2026 World Cup
Partnerships with schools, nonprofits and municipalities
one_sentence: Indoor sports facilities management is a fragmented local-services industry whose 2025-2026 recovery is being lifted by record sports participation, youth team sports, soccer, pickleball and paid facility usage, while labor, utilities and maintenance keep margins tight.

title: Industrial & Commercial Fan & Blower Manufacturing
one_liner: U.S. manufacturers of industrial air movement, ventilation, dust collection and stationary air purification equipment are benefiting from data centers, industrial construction and efficiency-driven retrofits, while steel, aluminum and import exposure keep margins tight.
overview: The industry is a mature, engineering-led machinery niche tied to private nonresidential construction, industrial production, HVAC replacement, air quality regulation and aftermarket parts. The 2021 IBISWorld baseline put revenue at $5.957 billion in 2021 and projected recovery to $6.8 billion in 2026, while public 2025 market estimates place the U.S. industrial and commercial fan and blower market near $6.9 billion in 2025. Demand is strongest where facilities need reliable air movement, cooling, filtration or process ventilation: data centers, warehouses, manufacturing plants, utilities, mining, cement, food processing, water treatment and commercial HVAC. The industry remains fragmented, but larger groups are gaining scale through acquisitions, digital monitoring, certified performance ratings and broader aftermarket networks.

key_stats.market_size: $6.9 billion U.S. market estimate in 2025 for industrial and commercial fans and blowers; IBIS baseline projected U.S. industry revenue of $6.8 billion in 2026.
key_stats.growth: 3.1% CAGR forecast for the U.S. industrial and commercial fans and blowers market from 2025 to 2032; IBIS baseline projected 2.5% annualized U.S. industry revenue growth from 2021 to 2026.
key_stats.establishments: 479 U.S. employer establishments in NAICS 333413 in 2023, according to Census Business Patterns.
key_stats.manufacturing_context: Federal Reserve data showed U.S. manufacturing output up 1.1% year over year in June 2026 and up at a 4.7% annual rate in Q2 2026.
key_stats.construction_context: Census estimated private nonresidential construction spending at a $738.7 billion seasonally adjusted annual rate in May 2026, down 0.3% from April 2026.

baseline_2022.market_size: Approximately $6.1 billion in 2022, inferred from the 2021 IBISWorld revenue base of $5.957 billion and its 2.5% annualized 2021-2026 revenue outlook.
baseline_2022.growth: Approximately 2.5% in 2022, using the 2021 IBISWorld 2021-2026 projected annualized growth rate.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers earn revenue from engineered and catalog sales of centrifugal fans and blowers, axial and roof ventilators, attic and commercial exhaust fans, dust and fume collection systems, air purification equipment, replacement motors, controls, impellers, dampers, housings, filters, bearings, service parts, repair work and system upgrades. Large projects are sold through direct engineering channels, OEM relationships, HVAC contractors, distributors and system integrators; higher-margin revenue comes from custom engineered units, certified energy-efficient models, replacement parts and aftermarket service.

cost_structure.materials_and_components: Steel, aluminum, motors, drives, bearings, electronics, fabricated housings, sheet metal, castings and filters are the largest cost exposures in 2025-2026, with 2025 Section 232 steel and aluminum tariff increases raising input-risk for import-dependent supply chains.
cost_structure.labor: IBISWorld estimated $1.253 billion of wages in 2021, equal to about 21.0% of 2021 revenue; skilled fabrication, welding, engineering, testing and service labor remain important constraints in 2025-2026.
cost_structure.profit: IBISWorld estimated a 5.1% profit margin in 2021 and projected 5.2% in 2026, indicating modest margins despite steady demand.
cost_structure.compliance_and_testing: Since the DOE fan and blower test procedure took effect in October 2023, manufacturers making energy-use representations in the U.S. must use the federal test method, increasing the value of certified ratings, lab testing and product documentation.
cost_structure.other_costs: Freight, energy, warranty, product testing, software-enabled selection tools, inventory, distributors and field service capacity are recurring costs in 2025-2026.

current_dynamics: Demand is being pulled in two directions in 2025-2026. Data centers, industrial modernization, reshoring-related factory work, utility and water projects, and indoor air quality retrofits support orders for high-efficiency fans, blowers and filtration systems. At the same time, broad private nonresidential construction is uneven, traditional office demand remains weak, and manufacturers face higher costs from steel, aluminum, electronics, motors and tariff uncertainty. Product selection is increasingly shaped by FEI ratings, energy-code adoption and total cost of ownership rather than first cost alone.
whats_growing: Data center ventilation and cooling support equipment, certified high-efficiency FEI-rated fans, variable-speed systems, EC motor and controls integration, replacement and retrofit demand in aging commercial buildings, dust and fume collection for industrial safety, wastewater aeration blowers, aftermarket monitoring and service, and products tied to energy, mining, cement, food processing and advanced manufacturing projects.
whats_shrinking: Commodity fan models with weak efficiency documentation, low-margin imports exposed to tariff and logistics risk, demand from traditional office construction, projects dependent on high-rate commercial real estate financing, older FEG-only specification practices, and manufacturers unable to support certified ratings or modern selection software.
recent_developments: 2023-10-30: DOE fan and blower test procedures took effect, making federal test-method compliance necessary for U.S. energy-use representations.

2025-01-17: DOE withdrew its January 2024 proposed energy conservation standards rule for fans and blowers, leaving no current federal energy conservation standard while the test procedure remains in force.
2025-06-04: U.S. steel and aluminum tariffs increased to 50% for most countries, raising 2025 input-cost and sourcing risk for metal-intensive fan and blower producers.
2026-01-23: Dodge Construction Network reported 2025 total construction starts up 5.4%, with nonbuilding construction and data centers as the main growth engines.
2026-07-16: Baker Hughes completed its acquisition of Chart Industries, bringing Howden air and gas handling assets into a larger industrial energy technology platform.
2026-07-17: Federal Reserve reported June 2026 manufacturing output was 1.1% above June 2025 and Q2 2026 manufacturing output rose at a 4.7% annual rate.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is moderately positive but cost-sensitive. Revenue should remain supported by data center buildouts, industrial and utility activity, plant modernization, clean-air compliance and energy-efficient retrofits. Margins are likely to stay uneven because steel and aluminum costs, tariffs, motor and electronics availability, freight, and skilled labor limit pricing flexibility for smaller manufacturers. Larger players with certified product lines, application engineering, controls, digital monitoring and aftermarket service should gain share, while smaller shops remain viable in custom niches but face more compliance and sourcing burden.
themes: Data center cooling and ventilation demand
Energy efficiency and FEI-rated product selection
Indoor air quality and dust/fume collection
Fragmented domestic manufacturing with selective consolidation

title: Industrial & Fluid Power Valve Manufacturing
one_liner: A mature flow-control manufacturing niche serving factories, water systems, energy, chemicals and aerospace, with 2026 demand improving after a soft 2025 industrial and drilling cycle.
overview: The industry manufactures industrial valves, hydraulic and pneumatic valves, flow-control devices, assemblies, couplings and fittings used in manufacturing plants, waterworks, municipal systems, refineries, chemical plants, oil and gas production, power generation, aerospace and mobile equipment. IBISWorld's 2022 baseline put industry revenue at $27.845 billion, with a forecast to reach $29.3 billion by 2027; applying that path implies roughly $28.7 billion in 2025 industry revenue. The broader US Valve Manufacturing industry, which also includes plumbing and other valve categories, was reported at $38.8 billion in 2025, so this narrower industrial and fluid-power segment remains the majority of the broader category. Current 2026 conditions are better than 2025: Federal Reserve data showed total industrial production 1.1% above June 2025 and manufacturing output 1.1% above June 2025, while Baker Hughes reported 587 US rigs on July 24, 2026, up 45 from a year earlier. Still, the market is not broad-based: public construction is supporting water and infrastructure demand, but total construction spending in May 2026 was 1.5% below May 2025, and machinery, industrial equipment and some energy customers remain uneven.

key_stats.market_size: Estimated $28.7 billion in US industry revenue in 2025, based on IBISWorld's 2022 revenue of $27.845 billion and 2022-2027 forecast path to $29.3 billion
key_stats.growth: Estimated roughly 1.0% annual revenue growth on the 2022-2027 IBISWorld forecast path; 2026 demand indicators improved with June 2026 manufacturing output up 1.1% year over year
key_stats.broader_market_context: Broader US Valve Manufacturing revenue was $38.8 billion in 2025, including industrial valves, plumbing fixture valves, fittings and trim, fluid power valves and other valves
key_stats.profit_margin: 8.6% industry profit margin in 2022 baseline; 2025-2026 margins pressured by steel, aluminum, copper and component tariffs but supported by higher-value severe-service and automated valves
key_stats.employment: 74,952 workers in 2022 baseline; broader US Valve Manufacturing employment was 82,578 in 2025
key_stats.establishments: 887 establishments in 2022 baseline; broader US Valve Manufacturing had 870 businesses in 2025
key_stats.exports: $9.277 billion in 2022 baseline, equal to 33.3% of 2022 revenue
key_stats.imports: $13.937 billion in 2022 baseline, equal to 42.7% of 2022 domestic demand
key_stats.demand_indicators: Federal Reserve: total industrial production index 102.6 in June 2026, up 1.1% from June 2025; manufacturing index 97.9 in June 2026, up 1.1% from June 2025; Baker Hughes: 587 US rigs on July 24, 2026, up 45 year over year

baseline_2022.growth: 2.4% CAGR over 2017-2022; 1.3% growth in 2022; IBISWorld forecast 1.0% CAGR to $29.3 billion by 2027

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers sell engineered industrial valves, gate/globe/check valves, ball/butterfly/plug valves, hydraulic and pneumatic valves, actuators, fittings, couplings, assemblies and replacement parts to OEMs, distributors, industrial plants, municipal utilities, energy producers and process industries. Revenue comes from initial equipment sales, configured or custom severe-service valves, aftermarket replacement parts, repair and service, and increasingly integrated valve automation, digital controllers and actuator packages. Pricing power is strongest in nuclear, aerospace, petrochemical, mining, severe-service, sanitary and automation-heavy applications where reliability, certification and downtime avoidance matter more than unit price; commodity valves face import-based price competition.
cost_structure: Costs are dominated by purchased materials and components, especially steel, stainless steel, castings, forgings, aluminum, copper-bearing parts, rubber, seals, electronics, actuators and machined components. Wages were $5.476 billion in 2022, about 19.7% of 2022 revenue, reflecting skilled machining, engineering, quality control and sales support. Profit was 8.6% of 2022 revenue. 2025-2026 metal tariffs and higher domestic steel, aluminum and copper costs raise input-cost risk, while Buy America rules can support domestic pricing in public water and infrastructure projects. Larger firms can defend margins through automation, global sourcing, aftermarket service, engineered product mix and scale purchasing; smaller shops are more exposed to working-capital swings and customer pushback on price increases.
current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 cycle is a tug-of-war between stronger infrastructure and industrial automation demand and weak spots in oil-and-gas drilling, construction and general industrial equipment. Federal Reserve data show manufacturing output in June 2026 was 1.1% above June 2025, a helpful turn for replacement and OEM valve demand, but manufacturing capacity utilization remained 75.7%, still below its long-run average. Energy demand is improving from the 2025 trough: EIA reported lower-48 rigs had declined from 750 in December 2022 to 517 in October 2025, while Baker Hughes later reported 587 US rigs on July 24, 2026, up 45 year over year. Water infrastructure remains structurally supportive because EPA programs, WIFIA funding, state revolving funds and Build America, Buy America requirements favor domestic iron, steel and manufactured products in federally funded projects. At the same time, import penetration remains a core challenge: lower-cost valves from Mexico, China and other suppliers keep pressure on commodity products, while 2025-2026 tariffs on steel, aluminum, copper and China-origin goods complicate both imported finished valves and domestic input costs.
whats_growing: Automated control valves, digital positioners, actuators and valves integrated into plant control systems; severe-service valves for mining, mineral extraction, LNG, refining, petrochemical and power applications; waterworks and municipal infrastructure valves tied to WIFIA, SRF and Build America, Buy America projects; aerospace and defense fluid-power applications; aftermarket replacement parts and service; domestic-content-qualified products for federally funded infrastructure; high-spec valves for nuclear, hydrogen, carbon capture, LNG and data-center-adjacent power and cooling infrastructure.
whats_shrinking: Commodity manual valves where imports compete mainly on price; oilfield valve demand tied to lower US drilling intensity versus the 2022 peak; lower-margin standard hydraulic products exposed to off-highway, transportation and in-plant equipment softness; small regional manufacturers without automation, certifications, working capital or purchasing scale; export competitiveness when the US dollar is strong; projects exposed to high interest rates or delayed private construction budgets.
recent_developments: 2025-04: IBISWorld reported broader US Valve Manufacturing revenue of $38.8 billion in 2025, with 1.1% CAGR over 2020-2025 and 870 businesses.
2025-06: US Section 232 steel and aluminum tariffs increased from 25% to 50% effective June 4, 2025, raising cost volatility for metal-intensive valve producers.
2025-10: EIA reported lower-48 oil and gas rigs had fallen from 750 in December 2022 to 517 in October 2025, reducing upstream valve demand despite production efficiencies.
2025-11: EPA announced $6.5 billion in newly available WIFIA funding plus $550 million for states, supporting water-system projects that use valves and flow-control equipment.
2026-04: The White House strengthened tariff assessment on steel, aluminum and copper products and derivatives, extending cost and sourcing uncertainty for valve supply chains.

2026-07: Federal Reserve reported June 2026 total industrial production up 1.1% year over year and manufacturing output up 1.1% year over year; Baker Hughes reported 587 US rigs on July 24, 2026, up 45 year over year.
outlook: The outlook is modestly positive rather than high-growth. Revenue should track low-single-digit growth through 2027 as industrial production, mining, water infrastructure, public works, power generation, chemicals and aerospace offset slower private construction and volatile oil-and-gas spending. The strongest operators will shift mix toward engineered severe-service valves, automation, actuators, digital controls and aftermarket service, where price competition is less intense. Domestic-content rules and tariffs can help some US producers win infrastructure work, but they also raise input costs and force customers to scrutinize project budgets. Imports will remain a durable constraint in standard products, so margin expansion depends more on product mix, service attachment, process automation and supply-chain discipline than on volume growth alone.
one_sentence: US industrial and fluid power valve manufacturers are recovering with industrial production and infrastructure demand, but import penetration, tariff-driven metal costs and volatile oil-and-gas spending keep growth modest.

title: Industrial Building Construction in the US
one_liner: Factory megaprojects lifted industrial builders after 2022, but the 2026 market is cooling from the CHIPS- and IRA-driven construction peak.
overview: The industry covers general contractors, design-build firms and construction managers responsible for new construction, additions, alterations, maintenance and repairs on industrial and manufacturing buildings. The 2022 IBIS baseline described a mature, low-concentration industry with revenue of $27.3 billion and 2022 growth of 0.4%, after pandemic disruption and weak manufacturing investment. Since then, public data show a major manufacturing construction boom, especially in semiconductor, battery, electric vehicle, electronics and clean-tech facilities, followed by visible cooling in 2026. U.S. Census/FRED manufacturing construction spending reached very elevated 2024-2025 levels but was $172.7 billion at a seasonally adjusted annual rate in June 2026, down from $214.1 billion in October 2025 and well below the reported 2024 annual average of $235.6 billion. Contractors still benefit from large backlogs and long-duration megaprojects, but margins are pressured by labor scarcity, high interest rates, schedule risk, equipment lead times and materials inflation.

key_stats.growth: 2026: roughly flat to slightly negative revenue growth as manufacturing construction spending slowed; Census/FRED manufacturing construction spending was $172.7 billion SAAR in June 2026 versus $214.1 billion in October 2025.

key_stats.profit_margin: 2022: 4.3% EBIT margin in the IBIS baseline; 2026 margins remain constrained by labor and material escalation.

how_it_makes_money.general_contracting_land_for_sale: 2022: 2.3% of revenue; contractors develop or partly finance buildings for sale or transfer.

cost_structure.subcontractors_and_materials: 2026: largest cost bucket; steel, concrete, electrical gear, HVAC, cleanroom systems and specialty trade subcontractors dominate project costs.
cost_structure.equipment_and_energy: 2026: cranes, earthmoving equipment, fuel, temporary power and rented equipment remain important variable costs on large sites.
cost_structure.profit: 2022: EBIT profit margin was 4.3%; 2026 margin risk is elevated where fixed-price bids did not fully pass through materials and labor inflation.
cost_structure.overhead: 2026: insurance, bonding, design coordination, permitting, safety compliance, project controls and administrative staff are meaningful but smaller than direct construction costs.

current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 market is shaped by a transition from boom to digestion. Semiconductor, battery, EV, pharmaceutical, food-processing and clean-tech projects created a surge in factory construction after 2022, but Census/FRED data show manufacturing construction spending falling through the first half of 2026. Builders with advanced manufacturing, cleanroom, process piping, power and mission-critical capabilities remain favored, while smaller generalists face thinner bid pipelines and more price competition. Higher financing costs have delayed speculative and discretionary industrial projects, while federal incentives and corporate supply-chain localization keep large strategic projects alive. Labor availability is a binding constraint on schedules, and contractors are using prefabrication, modular MEP racks, early procurement and construction-management-at-risk models to control risk.
whats_growing: 2025-2026 semiconductor fabs, advanced packaging, cleanrooms and electronics plants tied to CHIPS Act awards and AI supply chains.
2025-2026 battery, EV component, solar, grid-equipment and clean-tech manufacturing facilities supported by reshoring and energy-transition incentives.
2025-2026 pharmaceutical, biologics, food-processing and cold-chain industrial facilities with specialized HVAC, sanitary and process requirements.
2026 renovation, automation, resiliency and power-upgrade work inside existing plants, especially where new-build financing is harder.
whats_shrinking: 2026 broad manufacturing construction spending is declining from 2024-2025 highs, reducing new bid volume for less specialized builders.
2025-2026 speculative industrial projects are weaker where owners rely on debt financing and do not have committed tenants or production contracts.
2026 lower-complexity manufacturing buildings face more competition and more risk of relocation to lower-cost regions or Mexico.
2026 fixed-price work is less attractive as material, tariff and labor volatility increase contractor risk.

2025-12: GAO reported Commerce had awarded 19 companies $30.9 billion in CHIPS direct funding and $5.5 billion in loans for 40 semiconductor facility projects as of July 2025.

2026-07: CRS reported CHIPS-funded fab milestones run from November 2024 through October 2033, supporting a long but uneven construction pipeline.
2026-08: Census reported June 2026 total construction spending of $2.1665 trillion SAAR, down 3.2% from June 2025, while manufacturing construction spending was $172.7 billion SAAR.
outlook: Through 2027-2030, industrial building construction should remain above its pre-2022 baseline but below the 2024-2025 factory-construction peak. The strongest opportunities are in highly technical megaprojects that require cleanrooms, heavy electrical infrastructure, process utilities, water treatment, automation and power resilience. Growth will be uneven because semiconductor and battery projects are large, lumpy and politically exposed, while financing costs and construction input inflation limit ordinary plant expansions. Contractors with self-perform capability, strong trade networks, procurement discipline and balance-sheet capacity should gain share. The main downside risks are project postponements, incentive uncertainty, tariffs raising material costs, skilled-labor bottlenecks and weaker manufacturing utilization; upside comes from AI hardware demand, reshoring, defense supply chains and power-intensive industrial production.
